text: A 22-year-old photojournalist in Mumbai was gang-raped by five individuals, including a juvenile, on 22 August 2013, at the deserted Shakti Mills compound near Mahalaxmi in South Mumbai. She had gone on an assignment with a male colleague, and the accused tied up the colleague, raped the photojournalist, and used a broken beer bottle to hold her down, taking photos of her during the assault and threatening to release them online if she reported the crime. The perpetrators forced her to clean the scene and later brought her and her colleague to railway tracks around 7:15 pm, instructing them to stay. After the attackers left, the victim informed her colleague of being raped six times and needed medical help. They reached Mahalaxmi station, where her colleague contacted their boss and they went to Jaslok Hospital at Peddar Road. The victim, who was bleeding heavily, was admitted and began treatment. She gave a statement to police on 26 August and was discharged on 27 August. In a hospital statement, she expressed her desire for no other woman to face such humiliation, called for severe punishment, and stated she would continue fighting and return to work. Nirmala Samant Prabhawalkar of the National Commission for Women noted she was recovering but still traumatized. On 3 September, a 19-year-old telephone operator reported being gang-raped at the same Shakti Mills compound by five men on 31 July 2013, three of whom were also involved in the photojournalist case. Similar to the first incident, the attackers tied and beat the victim’s male companion before raping her, and the two victims fled to Chhattisgarh without reporting the crime due to fear. Mumbai Police conducted a "two-finger test" on the telephone operator despite a Maharashtra Government Resolution of 10 May 2013 that banned the test as degrading and medically irrelevant. Police formed 20 teams and involved officers from 12 crime branch units and 16 police stations. The five accused in the photojournalist case—Vijay Jadhav, Siraj Rehman Khan alias Sirju, Chand Shaikh, Mohamed Kasim Hafiz Sheikh alias Kasim, and Mohammed Salim Ansari—were arrested within 65 hours of the complaint being registered. Chand Shaikh was arrested on 23 August from Dhobi Ghat, Vijay Jadhav on 24 August from a video club, Siraj Rehman Khan on 24 August from a hideout in Govandi, Qasim Shaikh on 25 August outside Nair Hospital, and Salim Ansari on 25 August at the Delhi-Haryana border after fleeing to Delhi. The accused in the telephone operator case included Vijay Jadhav, Mohamed Kasim Hafiz Sheikh, Mohammed Salim Ansari, Mohammed Ashfaq Sheikh (26), and an unnamed minor. On 19 September 2013, the Mumbai crime branch filed charges against the four adults and a minor, including sections 376(d) for gang rape, 377 for unnatural offence, 120(b) for criminal conspiracy, 342 and 343 for wrongful restraint, 506(2) for criminal intimidation, 34 for common intention, and 201 for destruction of evidence. The prosecution also sought a charge under section 67A of the Information Technology Act against Ansari for showing porn clips to the survivor. The sessions court, presided over by Principal Sessions Judge Shalini Phansalkar-Joshi, ordered trial to begin on 14 October 2013 and was to be completed within 60 days. On 14 October, three independent witnesses testified; the photojournalist’s mother and boss gave statements, and the proceedings were held in-camera on the second and third days. On 17 October, the photojournalist identified her attackers in a four-hour deposition. On 30 October, the telephone operator testified, weeping and trembling, and recognized four of the five accused. On 20 November, her friend testified. On 13 January 2014, the photojournalist’s male colleague testified and identified all accused. On 20 March 2014, the sessions court convicted all five adult accused on 13 counts, including gang rape, destruction of evidence, wrongful restraint, assault, common intention, unnatural sex, criminal conspiracy, and charges under the Information Technology Act. The court awarded the death penalty to Vijay Jadhav, Qasim Shaikh, and Salim Ansari—repeat offenders in both cases—on 4 April 2014, marking the first time in India that such a sentence was given under section 376E of the IPC, introduced after the 2012 Delhi gang rape. Siraj Khan, the other convicted in the photojournalist case, was sentenced to life imprisonment. The judge emphasized the depravity of the accused, stating they enjoyed the assault, had no motive, and showed no remorse, and that the crime was premeditated and heinous. The court rejected arguments based on socioeconomic status or lack of physical injuries, noting the trauma and the need for deterrence. On 25 November 2021, the Bombay High Court commuted the death sentences of the three repeat offenders to life imprisonment. A division bench of Justices Sadhana Jadhav and Prithviraj Chavan ruled that section 376E is not a substantive offence but a punishment for repeat offenders under sections 376D, 376DA, and 376DB, and that death penalty is not mandatory. The court stated that death ends the possibility of repentance and that while the crime is heinous, it does not necessarily warrant the death penalty.

Jadhav and Prithviraj Chavan ruled that while setting aside the death penalty, it might appear to the public that the court is acting against the majority, but constitutional courts must follow established legal procedures rather than focusing solely on individual rights or the rights of the accused. They clarified that Section 376E of the Indian Penal Code is not a standalone substantive offence but a punishment for repeat offenders under Sections 376D, 376DA, and 376DB, and not necessarily for committing an offence after the first conviction as per Section 75 of the Indian Penal Code, but rather for cases tried after a prior conviction for a similar offence. The court noted that death penalty eliminates the possibility of repentance or mental suffering. Although acknowledging the heinous nature of the offence, the court stated that it cannot be assumed the accused deserve only the death penalty. Instead, it held that the convicts deserve rigorous imprisonment for life—meaning the remainder of their natural lives—without any remission, parole, or furlough, as their conduct, including their bold confession to the survivor that she was not the first victim, shows no possibility of reformation or rehabilitation. The court concluded that such individuals should not be reintegrated into society, as they view women with contempt, derision, and as objects of desire. Samajwadi Party (SP) MLA Naresh Agarwal (now in BJP) sparked controversy over the Mumbai gang-rape by suggesting women should pay attention to their clothing to avoid being raped and that they should not be overly influenced by television. In response to the verdict, the mother of the telephone operator stated that the convicts deserved death, as no harsher punishment would be fitting, and that their release would encourage further crimes and send a wrong message to society. She emphasized that equal urgency must be applied to all rape and molestation cases and shared how the incident has deeply affected her life, with neighbors taunting her and youths chasing her, especially during family outings. She also noted that the quick conviction was due to the proximity of the 2014 general elections. On 10 April 2014, SP chief Mulayam Singh Yadav said that when boys and girls have differences, the girl's statement that "the boy raped me" leads to the boy receiving a death sentence, and in reference to the Mumbai gang rape, he stated that after differences arose, the girl reported the rape, resulting in three men being sentenced to death. He claimed that rape cases should not lead to hanging, as boys make mistakes, and that two or three had been given death sentences in Mumbai. Complaints were filed against Yadav with the Election Commission and the National Commission for Women (NCW). His comments were denounced by the Indian media, women's groups, women's rights activists, public prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam in the Shakti Mills case, Bollywood celebrities, and many Uttar Pradesh residents. The Times of India criticized Yadav as having sunk to a new low, stating that the legal changes were the result of citizens' efforts to transform India's social outlook, and that calling rape a "mistake boys make" was a direct insult to those efforts. The parents of the 2012 Delhi gang rape victim strongly condemned Yadav, urging people not to vote for his party, with the victim's mother stating that rape is a crime, not a mistake, and that a leader making such remarks has no right to power. The remarks were criticized by both BJP and Congress politicians, some of whom demanded an apology from Yadav. Rashtriya Janata Dal President Lalu Prasad Yadav criticized Yadav, saying he had lost his mental balance and that there is no place for rapists in society. Political leaders like Raj Thackeray and Prime Minister candidate Narendra Modi condemned Yadav for his insensitive and anti-women views during appearances on Aap Ki Adalat. Mulayam was defended by his daughter-in-law Dimple Yadav, who stated such comments are made by many people and happen occasionally. Following a gang rape in Budaun district on 27 May 2014, United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon criticized Yadav, stating that the "boys will be boys" attitude is dismissive and destructive. After Yadav's comments, he and several SP leaders were labeled as "Supporters of Rape and Rapists". The day after Yadav's remarks, SP Maharashtra unit chief Abu Azmi told Mid-Day that any woman, whether married or unmarried, who goes along with a man with or without consent should be hanged, as rape is punishable by hanging in Islam, and that in this case, women are also guilty. He claimed that girls complain when touched, even when not touched, and that if rape occurs with or without consent, it should be punished as per Islamic law. He also said that he did not know the context of Yadav's statement, but that the wrong people are sometimes given the death penalty, and that boys commit such acts in "josh" (excitement), and that the death sentence should be given, adding that he would not speak against Islam. Azmi's comments were widely criticized across India.
